description: It swims through sand the way fish forget water. Only the jagged back-plates betray the tide beneath.
lore: The dunes are the one ground in this country that keeps nothing. Put a thing under them and the sand hands it back — a week later, a season later, standing on end in a clean hollow with a delver's wake still settling around it. The animal is not looking for your box. There is nothing on the front of it that is looking at anything; it goes through a dune the way something goes through water, on those pale spade-claws, and whatever was down there ends up on top.

[[characters/cfe826c1|Jehanne]] walked three days east of her rota last autumn and buried the bell she calls people to fire with. She tells the story herself, at her own fire, and tells it well: how she could not go on ringing a thing she had stopped believing in, and could not bring herself to break it either, and so put it under a dune and came home lighter than she had walked out. Eleven days. Then a charcoal burner turned up at her door with it, upright and clean and pleased with himself.

She rings it every evening now, and the story gets its laugh, and she lets it. What she leaves out is that anyone who has worked that country knows exactly what the dunes do with anything you put in them. She had been out there before. She chose the place.
gm_notes: Jehanne staged her own answer and knows it — she needed the bell handed back to her by somebody else so she could keep ringing it without deciding anything. Do not let another text resolve whether she admits this; the joke at her own expense IS the admission, and she is the only one who hears it that way. The delver itself is a plain animal with a habit and no intent, and should stay that way: it is the country refusing to let anyone put a thing down, not a helper.
